newsitem.title: JAPAN: Fujitsu seen suffering from PC business losses.
newsitem.headline: Fujitsu seen suffering from PC business losses.

text.p: A crash in memory chip prices and a cloudy earnings outlook have rattled Fujitsu Ltd's personal computer business, analysts said.

Fujitsu, which has made an impressive foray into the PC market in Japan over the past three years with aggressive pricing, is being forced to change its hawkish marketing policy after profits from the chip business plunged and losses from PC sales mounted, analysts say.
"Necessity knows no law, and Fujitsu needed to turn its eyes more to profits from market share," said Naoki Sato, an analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
The company recently raised prices on its consumer-use, low-end PC lineup in Japan by 10,000 yen ($90) -- the first rise since it launched an all-out offensive on Japan's PC market two years ago.

Analysts have been quick to interpret the price rise as an admission that the firm is worried about profitability in its PC business. The chip business no longer yields generous profits to make up for PC losses.

Computer chip prices have fallen to one-fifth the level they were at early this year and some analysts believe the plunge will nullify profits in Fujitsu's chip business in the year to next March, down from an estimated 130 billion yen ($1.18 billion) profit last business year.
Fujitsu officials said there is no change in its marketing policy and denied industry talk that handsome profits from the chip business are behind the aggressive PC sales strategy.
"Our basic strategy has not changed," a Fujitsu spokesman said.
Fujitsu officials said they were looking at their computer division, including mainframes, PCs, software and networking products, as a whole and not just at PCs.
But some analysts said Fujitsu at least has achieved its initial sales target and it is possible to review its policy now that its PC sales in Japan have topped two million.
"The big presence provides it with a platform for expanding and launching new computer business," said Hiroyuki Iba, analyst at Nikko Research Center.

In less than three years, Fujitsu, with its competitively priced products, has become the biggest manufacturer of IBM-compatible PCs in Japan, putting international giants like International Business Machines Co and Compaq Computer KK in the shade.
Research company IDC Japan estimates Fujitsu's 1995 market share in Japan's 5.76 million PC market at 18.4 percent, the second biggest after NEC Corp.
NEC, which had a 40.1 percent share, sells PCs that use its own architecture, which can run Windows-compatible software.
Fujitsu, which used to sell PCs using a proprietary architecture, jumped into the camp of IBM-compatible PCs, the de facto international standard, in November 1993.

Fujitsu's proprietary architecture sales had been limited to a specific customer base and the change opened sales possibilities to a wider range of customers and helped it compete better with major international rivals.
Just a few years ago, few would have believed that Fujitsu would adopt such a strategy.
Fujitsu and other Japanese computer makers traditionally developed PCs compatible only with their own architecture in order to create a client base that would not defect to other makers.
But after Fujitsu switched to IBM-compatibles, sales rose dramatically.
The company sold 450,000 IBM-compatible PCs in the first year and boosted sales to 1.45 million in the second year.
"We expect sales to well exceed two million, probably reach the 2.1 million mark, in the current year to end-March 1997," a Fujitsu spokeswoman said.
The explosive sales growth stems from a big price advantage. Industry officials say Fujitsu's products are about 50,000 yen ($454) cheaper than similar products sold in Japan.
Fujitsu's IBM-compatible FMV Deskpower is sold at just slightly above 200,000 yen ($1,818) and comes with more than 30 popular titles installed.
Despite the brisk sales, analysts said Fujitsu is not making profits from PCs and likely suffered losses of as much as 10 billion yen ($90.9 million) last year in its PC business.
Fujitsu does not disclose details of its PC sales income and costs.
Senior Fujitsu executives have said in the past that sudden declines in retail prices make it difficult for the company to generate profits.
Even with such a large loss, analysts say Fujitsu had to move aggressively into the PC market to protect its core business, which is information processing.

As more and more firms switch from expensive mainframe computers to PCs and workstations amid the downsizing trend, Fujitsu has been forced to increase its presence in the PC market or else could lose out in providing computer services.

Services are key for mainframe providers because they raise profits from software and technical maintenance sales. In the new age, PCs are required to be part of the network that links to the mainframes.
"There is no future for Fujitsu if it loses in the PC battle," said Kiyoshi Kimura, an analyst at Societe General.

Fujitsu is Japan's biggest mainframe maker and the second-largest in the world after IBM. The downsizing trend from big mainframes to PCs had put Fujitsu into the red in the 1992 and 1993 business years. The mainframe business until just recently was very unstable.
Fujitsu now relies on the overall computer business for 70 percent of its sales, including PCs, mainframes, software, maintenance and network-related services.
Analysts expect Fujitsu's computer division to post profits in the second half of the current business year helped by the recent retail price rises for PCs.
For the 1996/97 year, ending next March, Sato expects the division to yield operating profits of 33.8 billion yen ($307 million), or about 30 percent of total operating profits.
He estimates the division posted a loss of 100 million yen ($909,000) in the last business year.
"The PC price rises will improve its profitability, although there is a chance that Fujitsu will lose market share," Sato said.
Competitors Toshiba Corp and Mitsubishi Electric Corp are eager to rip away Fujitsu's market share by offering their own inexpensive desktop PCs. ($1=110 yen)
